composition: The material is SPCC mild steel (low-carbon steel sheet) in 1.2 mm thickness; the paper reports only this commercial designation and gives no quantitative chemical analysis, no element concentrations in wt% or at%. The matrix is ferritic Fe, and the deformation-mechanism discussion implies the presence of dissolved carbon and other solutes capable of locking dislocations (Cottrell atmosphere) in the annealed state. No alloying-element design intent is stated beyond the standard SPCC sheet specification.
conclusions: The annealed specimen E acts as the reference "dislocation-locked" state of the SPCC sheet: it has the highest elastic modulus of the five species studied (224 over 0–0.05% strain and 206 over the whole elastic range) and is the only specimen whose apparent modulus remains essentially unchanged up to yielding, with its modulus-versus-strain curve staying near 200 GPa before dropping. Comparison with the as-received, pre-strained and heat-treated variants supports the paper's central conclusion that the apparent elastic modulus decreases with increasing plastic strain and that movable dislocations, together with the pile-up of dislocations near grain boundaries, are the major cause of this decrease. The macroscopic behaviour of the apparent modulus was corroborated by microscopic nano-indentation showing a lower modulus near grain boundaries. Because the study further shows that a strain-dependent elastic modulus predicts experimental V-bending spring-back far better than a constant modulus, the annealed-state modulus data of specimen E provide the practical upper-bound benchmark needed for more accurate spring-back prediction in sheet metal forming.
mechanisms: Annealing removes the freely movable dislocations by letting carbon and other solutes re-lock them in Cottrell atmospheres, so in the annealed specimen E the apparent elastic modulus stays almost constant right up to macroscopic yielding — the only species among A–E for which this holds, whereas the as-received and pre-strained specimens show a modulus that decays from the very start of loading.

During plastic deformation dislocations are torn away from the Cottrell atmospheres and move under lower internal stress; they cannot be re-locked at room temperature because the diffusion rate of C in the Fe matrix is very low, so the change in dislocation structure is effectively irreversible.

Dislocations released from a common source glide on the same slip plane and pile up against obstacles such as grain boundaries and solutes; when the applied shear stress is released during unloading the pile-up dislocations can move backwards, producing additional deformation during unloading and even during loading at stresses below the yield stress.

Because the piled-up/movable dislocations at the grain boundary accommodate part of the deformation elastically irreversibly, the apparent (macroscopic) elastic modulus decreases, and the decrease grows with increasing plastic strain.

The measured modulus taken over the narrow initial strain window (0–0.05%) is systematically higher than that taken over the whole elastic range, the gap being smallest for specimen D (189/189) and the annealed specimen E (224/206) and largest for the pre-strained B and C (188/186 vs 162/162) — consistent with movable dislocations progressively lowering the apparent modulus as strain increases.

Microscopic nano-indentation shows the elastic modulus immediately next to a grain boundary to be lower than in the grain interior, confirming that the modulus reduction is localised where dislocation pile-up occurs and providing a micro-scale counterpart to the macroscopic modulus loss.

Alternative explanations for the modulus loss — increased residual stress, micro-cracks and a density reduction produced by plastic deformation — are considered but rejected as the dominant cause, because the density reduction caused by plastic deformation is less than 1% and cannot account for the observed magnitude of the modulus drop.

Introducing the strain-dependent (varied) elastic modulus into the V-bending FEM simulation reproduces the measured spring-back much more closely than a constant initial modulus, demonstrating that the modulus degradation is a controlling factor for spring-back in sheet forming.
microstructure: The annealed specimen is a polycrystalline mild-steel sheet consisting of grains separated by grain boundaries, with an Fe matrix. In this annealed state the dislocations in the Fe matrix are locked by carbon and other solutes through the Cottrell effect before any plastic deformation, so the material contains essentially no freely movable dislocations. No grain size, phase fraction, texture or precipitate data are reported for specimen E. The microstructural features most relevant to the study are (i) the grain boundaries, which act as obstacles to dislocation motion, and (ii) the pile-up configuration of dislocations against these boundaries (Fig. 3 model), which is the general micro-mechanism the paper invokes; nano-indentation across a boundary showed a lower elastic modulus immediately adjacent to the boundary than in the grain interior, with different grains sitting at different modulus levels because of their different orientations.
processing: Specimen E is defined in Table 1 simply as "Annealed" for the SPCC sheet of 1.2 mm thickness; it is the only heat-treatment/softening condition in the five-species series. Crucially, the paper does not report the annealing temperature, holding time, atmosphere or cooling medium for this condition, so the thermal path of specimen E beyond the word "annealed" is undocumented. Its processing history therefore cannot be reconstructed beyond: mill-received SPCC coil/sheet → annealing (parameters unreported) → tensile specimen. For context on the paper's other heat treatment: a separate recovery treatment of 373 K for 90 h was applied in the study to release only the Cottrell atmosphere while keeping dislocations stationary, but that condition corresponds to species C and D, not to the annealed specimen E.
properties: Mechanical (elastic) behaviour was measured by a tensile test using a load cell and a strain gauge, the stress–strain curve being recorded up to 1% strain and the elastic modulus extracted from the elastic deformation region. For the annealed specimen E the elastic modulus (no unit is printed in Table 2) was 224 when calculated over the strain region 0–0.05% and 206 when calculated over the whole elastic range; these are the highest values of all five species (A: 182/173, B: 188/162, C: 186/162, D: 189/189). In Fig. 4(a) the stress–strain curves of A–E overlap below about 0.05% strain and then diverge, the lowest curve plateauing near 225 MPa at 0.3% strain; in Fig. 4(b) the apparent elastic modulus versus strain, curve E remains near 200 GPa before dropping. Uniquely among A–E, the modulus of the annealed specimen stayed almost the same until yielding, i.e. its gradient did not decay from the very beginning of loading as it did for the as-received and pre-strained specimens. No yield strength, tensile strength, elongation, hardness, fatigue, creep or physical/chemical property values are reported for this specimen. Characterisation techniques applied in the study were (i) tensile testing with a load cell and strain gauge, and (ii) nano-indentation with a spherical indenter tip (Triboscope, Hysitron Inc., mounted on an SPM-9500J2 AFM stage; force range 1–10 mN with 100 nN sensitivity, displacement range 5 μm with 0.2 nm sensitivity), used with a nominal R = 50 μm (and R = 200 μm) spherical tip to keep the surface deformation elastic, on CMP-prepared surfaces, with points taken at about 1 μm intervals along lines crossing a grain boundary.
summary: Specimen E is the annealed condition of a 1.2 mm thick SPCC mild-steel sheet, one of five species (A–E) defined in Table 1 of a study on how plastic deformation alters material properties: A "as received", B "with 15% pre-strain", C "heat-treated after 15% pre-strain", D "heat-treated after received" and E "annealed". It serves as the fully softened, as-annealed reference state in a tensile study whose aim was to quantify the strain-induced decrease of the apparent elastic modulus and its influence on spring-back, combining macroscopic stress–strain measurements with microscopic nano-indentation.
unmapped: The annealing temperature, time, atmosphere and cooling conditions for specimen E are not reported anywhere in the paper; only the label 'Annealed' appears in Table 1.

The nano-indentation marker-location figure (Fig. 10) is labelled 'SPCE', whereas specimen E belongs to the SPCC material of Table 1; the nano-indentation results reported here may therefore pertain to a different (SPCE) specimen and should not be attributed to specimen E without qualification.

The paper's precision-extensometer large-deformation tensile tests (Section 2) and the V-bending spring-back FEM simulation were performed on SPCE sheet metal, not on the SPCC material to which specimen E belongs; the 373 K/90 h recovery heat treatment described in Section 2 corresponds to species C and D, not to the annealed specimen E.
No units for the elastic modulus are printed in Table 2; the values 224 and 206 are tabulated without units.
